newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says it has Turkish assurances on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says it has Turkish assurances on Iraq.

text.p: Egypt said on Monday it had Turkish assurances Turkey would not set up a military presence in Iraq.
Egyptian state radio said Turkish President Suleyman Demirel gave the assurances to President Hosni Mubarak when Mubarak called him by telephone on Monday morning.

"President Demirel assured President Mubarak that Turkey does not have a single soldier on Iraqi soil... Demirel also said that Turkey has no plans for a military presence on Iraqi territory," the radio said.

"The military moves Turkey is making are in the context of securing the Turkish border against terrorist and infiltration operations... and the Turkish forces are carrying out their missions inside Turkish territory," it said Demirel added.
The Egyptian report did not distinguish between a permament Turkish presence and short-term incursions to attack rebels of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK).
In its account Demirel's office said: "President Demirel gave information to his counterpart on the temporary danger zone that Turkey has declared on the Iraqi border.

Much of the Arab world has condemned a Turkish bid to set up a security zone in northern Iraq up to 10 km (six miles) deep to prevent attacks by Turkish Kurd rebels based on the Iraqi side of the border. Washington has tacitly backed the plan.
Mubarak, in comments published on Monday, warned against partitioning Iraq or annexing Iraqi territory.

"Iraq is an Arab state the survival and unity of which we are intent on preserving," Mubarak told the ruling party newspaper Mayo. "Partitioning Iraq would create a dangerous situation in the whole region," he added.
Turkey has said a security zone, which would be temporary, is needed to prevent infiltration by PKK rebels using bases there for its 12-year-old insurgency in southeast Turkey.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Sunday that Turkey ultimately planned to monitor Kurdish rebel activity in northern Iraq with an electronic system, eliminating any need to keep troops there.
